title: Solid treble square motif
subtitle: A dense three-round square worked from the centre out
excerpt: A solid square worked in rounds of treble, with no gaps between the clusters. Three rounds make a firm 10 cm square in DK cotton, the building block for a denser blanket than the open granny gives. Worked from a magic-ring centre out to four crisp corners.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the crochet square worked in rounds (Fig. 441). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. The magic-ring start and the DK-cotton gauge are modernised; the corner-and-side round structure is Victorian.

chartDefinition.title: Solid treble square, three rounds
chartDefinition.caption: Read each round outward from the magic-ring centre. The chain-2 spaces sit at the four corners; the sides fill solid with treble.

glossaryTerms.definition: An adjustable starting loop for working in the round. The first round is worked into the ring, then the tail is pulled to close the centre tight with no hole.
The gap left under one or more chains. Here the chain-2 spaces become the four corners of the square; later rounds work into the space.
Wetting or steaming the finished motif and pinning it square while it dries, so the corners sit true and the same size as every other square.

content.text: This square is worked solid, with treble filling every stitch and no gaps between the groups, so it makes a firmer, warmer fabric than the open granny square. Three rounds give a 10 cm square in DK cotton, the standard building block for a dense blanket or a cushion front. It starts from a
magic ring
and grows outward to four corners. The pattern is written in UK terms, where treble is the tall everyday stitch (double crochet in the United States).
What you need
DK cotton, one colour.
About 18 m makes one square. A mercerised DK cotton such as Drops Paris or Scheepjes Cahlista gives the cleanest stitch definition. Any DK yarn works, though cotton holds the square shape best.
A 4 mm hook.
The standard DK pairing. Drop to 3.5 mm if your tension runs loose, or go up to 4.5 mm if it runs tight, to hit the 10 cm size.
Tapestry needle, scissors, and a blocking surface.
For weaving in the tails and setting the square true.
Gauge

Rounds 1 to 3 make a square about 10 cm across in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook, blocked. The first round should measure about 4 cm across. If a single square comes off the wrong size, every join in a finished blanket is thrown out, so check it before making a full set.
Abbreviations
ch = chain
tr = treble (UK), called double crochet in the US
sl st = slip stitch
sp = space; st, sts = stitch, stitches
Pattern
Read the chart from the centre outward, alongside the written rounds. The chart shows the corners and sides; the written rounds give the counts.
Round 1.

Form a magic ring. Ch 3 (counts as the first treble), 2 tr into the ring, ch 2, [3 tr into the ring, ch 2] 3 times. Sl st to the top of the ch 3 to join, then pull the tail to close the ring. This makes four groups of 3 tr with a
chain space
at each corner. (12 sts)
Round 2.

Sl st into the next ch-2 corner space. Ch 3 (counts as the first treble), then 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr all into the same corner space. [1 tr in each of the next 3 tr, then work 3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr all into the next ch-2 corner space] 3 times. 1 tr in each of the next 3 tr. Sl st to the top of the ch 3 to join. (36 sts)
Round 3.

Sl st into the next ch-2 corner space. Ch 3 (counts as the first treble), then 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr all into the same corner space. [1 tr in each of the next 9 tr, then work 3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr all into the next ch-2 corner space] 3 times. 1 tr in each of the next 9 tr. Sl st to the top of the ch 3 to join. (60 sts)
Fasten off, leaving a 10 cm tail. The square is complete.
Finishing

Weave the start and end tails into the back of the work with the tapestry needle, doubling back once to lock each, then trim. Pin the square to a blocking surface, easing the four corners to a true 10 cm square, and
block
it. Cotton sets crisply and holds its shape once dry.
What to try next

Keep going for a fourth round, working 15 tr along each side between the corners, for a 13 cm square. Make a stack of squares the same size and join them with a slip-stitch seam or a whipstitch to build a dense blanket. Worked in a single colour the solid square reads calm and modern; worked in stripes it shows the rounds as bold frames.
